                                                         Abstract
     We study the problem of learning a structured approximation (low-rank, sparse, banded, etc.) to an
     unknown matrix A given access to matrix-vector product (matvec) queries of the form x 7→ Ax
     and x 7→ AT x. This problem is of central importance in scientific computing and machine learning,
     with applications to structured matrix compression, preconditioning, and as a theoretical model for
     operator learning. Prior work focuses on obtaining query complexity upper and lower bounds for
     learning specific structured matrix families that commonly arise in applications.
          We initiate the study of the problem in greater generality, aiming to understand the query
     complexity of learning approximations from general matrix families. Our main result focuses on
     finding a near-optimal approximation to A from any finite-sized family of matrices, F. Standard
     results from matrix sketching show that O(log |F|) matvec queries suffice in this setting. This
     bound can also be achieved, and is optimal, for vector-matrix-vector queries of the form x, y 7→
     xT Ay, which have been widely studied in work on rank-1 matrix sensing.

1. Introduction
What can we learn about an unknown matrix A from multiplying it by a few vectors? This ba-
sic question has been central to numerical linear algebra for decades, underlying work on Krylov
subspace methods (Saad, 2003, 2011), matrix sketching (Woodruff, 2014; Drineas and Mahoney,
2016), randomized numerical linear algebra (Weiße et al., 2006; Martinsson and Tropp, 2020), and
more. In its most general form, the task is to interact with an n × n matrix A in an adaptive way,
issuing matrix-vector product queries (“matvec queries”) of the form:

1.1. Matrix Approximation
One of the most important problems studied in the matvec query model is that of learning a near-
optimal approximation to A from a given “hypothesis class” of structured matrices, F. For example,
F could be all rank-k matrices or all tridiagonal matrices. We consider this problem in the agnostic
learning setting, where A is not assumed to lie in F, nor is it assumed to be generated from some
“true” matrix in F, e.g., by adding i.i.d. noise. Instead, we consider:

Problem 1 For an unknown A ∈ Rn×n and a matrix family F ⊂ Rn×n (a hypothesis class), find
B̃ ∈ F satisfying

for some approximation factor γ ≥ 1, using as few matvec queries to A and AT as possible.1

In other words, our goal is to find an approximation, B̃, from the class F that is competitive with
the best possible approximation to A in F. We measure error with respect to the Frobenius norm,
which is a popular choice. However, other matrix norms have also been considered (Kressner et al.,
2019; Musco and Musco, 2015). The problem is interesting in several possible regimes for γ: when
γ is close to 1 (i.e., γ = 1 + ϵ for some small ϵ), when γ is a constant, or even when γ is allowed to
grow slowly in n or other problem parameters (Amsel et al., 2026b; Le et al., 2025).
    Problem 1 arises in dozens of applications where the goal is to efficiently obtain an explicit
surrogate for an implicit operator. Examples include when A is the Hessian of a large-scale op-
timization problem, for which matvecs can be computed much more efficiently than realizing the
matrix (Pearlmutter, 1994; Dauphin et al., 2015), when A is the inverse of another matrix and we
wish to develop a fast solver (Lin et al., 2011; Martinsson, 2016), and when A is the solution op-
erator of a differential equation (Boullé and Townsend, 2023). For these applications, prior work
studies query complexity for a variety of structured families, like hierarchically structured matrices,
sparse matrices, butterfly matrices, and more.
    Problem 1 is also relevant when the goal is to replace an already explicit A with a structured

Beyond Specific Matrix Families. It is natural to ask if a more general theory exists for the
query complexity of structured matrix approximation. In supervised learning, a rich theory based
on VC dimension, pseudodimension, fat-shattering dimension, etc. helps categorize the complexity
of learning functions from arbitrary hypothesis classes (Pollard, 1990; Alon et al., 1997; Vapnik,
2000). Does a comparable theory exist for characterizing structured matrix families?
    This question is interesting because Problem 1 differs in important ways from standard super-
vised learning. First, as in active learning, data collection can be incremental and adaptive. More
interestingly, the output corresponding to any query/data example x ∈ Rn is itself an n dimensional
vector, Ax (or AT x). We might therefore hope to learn more from each example than in a setting
with scalar-valued outputs (informally, up to n times more). One such setting with scalar outputs
is “rank-1 matrix sensing”, a well-studied problem in compressed sensing. The goal is to learn an
approximation to A from queries of the form xT Ay (Zhong et al., 2015; Dasarathy et al., 2015;
Kueng et al., 2017)2 . We refer to this setting as the “vector-matrix-vector” query model.
    For many of the families mentioned above, there is a lot to be gained from the multidimensional
output. Rank-k matrices, for example, require O(nk) parameters to represent, and Ω(nk) vector-
matrix-vector queries to learn (Candes and Plan, 2011), but can be learned (up to constant accuracy)
using just O(k) matvec queries (Sarlos, 2006). Similarly, matrices with s non-zeros per row have
O(ns) parameters and require Ω(ns) vector-matrix-vector queries to learn (Dasarathy et al., 2015),
but just O(s) matvec queries (Amsel et al., 2026a). In both of these examples, matvec queries allow
for a dramatic n-factor improvement over scalar queries. Similar improvements are known for other
classes (Chen et al., 2025; Amsel et al., 2026b). What sort of improvement is possible in general?

1.2. Our Contributions
In this work, we take a step towards understanding the power of matvec queries for structured
matrix-approximation in greater generality by considering arbitrary finite families of matrices (i.e.,
with finite size |F|). Such families require log(|F|) bits (i.e., parameters) to represent, and it can
be shown using standard techniques that it is always possible to solve Problem 1 with constant
approximation factor γ using O(log |F|) matvec queries (see Section 2.1 for more details). Indeed,
this bound can be achieved in the more restrictive vector-matrix-vector setting, with queries of the
form xT Ay. In that setting, the bound is optimal (see Appendix D).
Upper Bound. Our main result shows that O(log |F|) is far from optimal for matvec queries.
By taking advantage of the multidimensional output of such queries, we give a nearly quadratic

Appendix A. Additional Related Work
While we believe our work is the first to address Problem 1 for general matrix families, as discussed,
the problem of learning a matrix from matvec queries has been studied extensively for specific struc-
tured families, F. We summarize this work below, along with additional related work in slightly
different models of computation.
Low-Rank Approximation. One of the most familiar settings is when F is the class of rank-k
matrices for some parameter k. The query complexity of rank-k approximation has been studied
extensively in numerical analysis and theoretical computer science: work on the randomized SVD
and related methods (Halko et al., 2011; Woodruff, 2014; Musco and Musco, 2015) has culminated
in a state-of-the-art upper bound of O(k/ϵ1/3 ) queries to achieve approximation factor γ = 1 + ϵ
for solving Problem 1 (Bakshi et al., 2022; Meyer et al., 2024). Our best known lower bound for
rank-k approximation is Ω(k + 1/ϵ1/3 ) (Bakshi and Narayanan, 2023).
Sparse Approximation. There has also been interest in families with a fixed pattern of s non-zeros
per row, for a parameter s. Such families including diagonal (s = 1), banded, and block diagonal
matrices (Bekas et al., 2007; Tang and Saad, 2011; Baston and Nakatsukasa, 2022; Dharangutte
and Musco, 2023). Matching upper and lower bounds of Θ(s/ϵ) queries are known for achieving
approximation factor γ = 1 + ϵ in this setting (Amsel et al., 2026a). Extensive work has also con-
sidered sparse matrices with unknown sparsity patterns (Curtis et al., 1974; Coleman and Cai, 1986;
Coleman and Moré, 1983; Wimalajeewa et al., 2013; Schäfer and Owhadi, 2024; Park and Nakat-
sukasa, 2026). Sparse matrix approximation finds applications in a variety of settings. One example
is in first-order optimization, where methods for learning diagonal and sparse approximations to a
Hessian matrix (for which x 7→ Ax can often computed efficiently using automatic differentiation
(Pearlmutter, 1994)) are used to implement quasi-second-order methods or to construct precondi-
tioners (Bordes et al., 2009; Dauphin et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2020).
Hierarchical and Block Structured Matrices. In computational science, more complex classes
of structured matrices are also important. For example, among other applications (Ambartsumyan
et al., 2020), methods for approximation via hierarchical low-rank matrices (HODLR, HSS, etc.)
can be used to construct fast direct solvers for integral equations given access to an implicit solver,
like a fast multipole method. Algorithms for learning such matrices from a small number of matvec
queries, as well as related block low-rank approximations, have been studied heavily in recent years
(Lin et al., 2011; Martinsson, 2016; Levitt and Martinsson, 2024a,b; Pearce et al., 2025). Such
matrices are also studied in scientific machine learning (SciML), where rank-structured matrix ap-
proximation has been utilized to learn the solution operators of linear PDEs given input/output
pairs (Boullé and Townsend, 2023; Boullé et al., 2023; Wang and Townsend, 2025; Boullé and
Townsend, 2024; Boullé et al., 2024). Relatedly, there has been work on learning butterfly matrices
from matvecs, which can be characterized by a so-called “complementary low-rank” property (Li
et al., 2015; Li and Yang, 2017; Liu et al., 2021).
     Two recent papers established the first multiplicative error bounds in the agnostic setting of
Problem 1 for HODLR and HSS matrices, two important subclasses of hierarchical low-rank matri-
ces (Chen et al., 2025; Amsel et al., 2026b).
Different Models. Beyond matvec query algorithms, there has been extensive work on learning
structured matrices (typically, sparse or low-rank) from linear measurements of the form tr(AM)
for a measurement matrix M (Waters et al., 2011; Candes and Plan, 2011; Kacham and Woodruff,
2023). Most related to our work is the setting when M is restricted to be rank-1, i.e., M = yxT

tr(AM) = xT Ay, so the problem is equivalent to learning from vector-matrix-vector queries,
which have been studied more broadly as a model for linear algebraic computation (Rashtchian
et al., 2020; Wimmer et al., 2014). A model that sits in between vector-matrix-vector and matrix-
vector queries is the one-sided matvec model, where we can only access A via multiplication on
the right (i.e., queries of the form x 7→ Ax, but not x 7→ AT x). This model arises in some settings,
including some operator learning problems in SciML, where it may not be possible to efficiently
compute AT x (Boullé et al., 2024).
    While stronger than the vector-matrix-vector model, we argue in Appendix D that Ω(log |F|)
one-sided matvec queries are still needed to learn a generic finite family F (i.e., quadratically worse
than what is possible via Theorem 1 with two-sided queries). This gap is intuitive: let F be a finite
net over the set of matrices whose first row is an arbitrary unit vector, and whose remaining rows
are all zero. This family has size 2O(n) , but we require n one-sided queries to learn a meaningful
approximation – we essentially need to read each entry in A’s first row. If two-sided queries are
allowed, we could multiply the first standard basis vector by AT to learn the first row with a single
query.
    Finally, regardless of the specific query model studied, many of the works above focus on the
non-agnostic or exact recovery setting, where A is assumed to be contained in our family F, i.e.
minB∈F ∥A−B∥F = 0. The goal is to exactly identify A – see e.g., Halikias and Townsend (2023).
For many matrix classes, the easier exact recovery problem has been tackled first, preceding results
in the agnostic setting. In a preliminary version of this paper (Amsel et al., 2025), we prove exact
recovery results for arbitrary finite families using an algorithm that is similar, but simpler, than the
one used to prove Theorem 1.
